summary: A Forest Service lookout on a Deschutes cinder cone, first built in 1931; the 1998 reproduction has a visitor center and is reached by shuttle in summer.

facts.design: 1998 reproduction of a gable-roofed L-4 cab with catwalk; first floor is a visitor center

access.note: First floor is a visitor center. Summer shuttle runs from the Lava Lands Visitor Center. The sources read do not say whether the cab itself is open to visitors.

visit.trail_note: Shuttle runs up Red Cinder Road from early May to mid October; hiking the road is possible all year; a rim trail about 0.35 miles long circles the top.

events.note: First Forest Service lookout on the summit, an L-4 groundhouse
Steep single-lane road built up the cone to the summit
Larger lookout with a slant-window flat-top cab replaced the 1931 tower
Enlarged to hold a small visitor center and museum on the first floor (Wikipedia). Firelookout.com dates the first-floor expansion to 1960
Structure dismantled to make way for a new lookout and visitor center
Current third structure on the site, a reproduction of a gable-roofed L-4 cab with catwalk
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register as Number 100

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register ties a downstairs visitor center to the 1957 cab. Firelookout.com dates the first-floor expansion to 1960. Wikipedia dates the enlargement that added a visitor center and museum to 1962. The story reports all three.
The register calls it a slant-window flat-top. Firelookout.com calls it a two-story flat cab. Both describe a flat roof, so they are read as the same design, described differently.
The register says the station is a visitor center for the Lavalands National Monument. Wikipedia places Lava Butte in the Newberry National Volcanic Monument. The story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Core dates (1931 first lookout, 1998 current structure, 2003 register) agree across all three pages. Open: staffing and whether the cab is open to visitors are not established by any page read. Elevation differs slightly (NHLR 4,958 ft; Firelookout.com 5016 ft; Wikipedia summit 5,020 ft) and was left out of the story. A search snippet suggested a 1913 telephone line and an earlier cabin; the full page was not read, so it is not used. The brief's record of a 1998 build is correct for the present tower but omits the 1931 original.
